Question: What made you want to do this now?
Why we ask: The trigger tells us what the sponsor will judge the work on.
Follow-up probes: A recent incident, a new hire, a board ask?
Good answer looks like: A specific trigger.

Question: If this goes well, what is different in finance in 12 months?
Why we ask: Anchors the recommendation in the sponsor's own outcomes.
Follow-up probes: Push for two or three concrete outcomes
Good answer looks like: Two or three concrete outcomes.
Red flags: Only 'use AI' with no business outcome.

Question: How will you judge whether it was worth it? Do we have a baseline today?
Why we ask: Gives baselines and targets for success measures.
Follow-up probes:
Hours, errors, days to close?
Who tracks it today?
Good answer looks like: A measure with a baseline.
Red flags: No measure anyone tracks.

Question: Which processes matter most?
Why we ask: Selects the intake modules; anything without a module uses GEN.
Follow-up probes:
Why those?
Who owns each?
Good answer looks like: A short ranked list of processes, each mapped to a module.
Red flags: Too many processes for the fee.

Question: Is there anything we should deliberately leave out (e.g. payroll, tax, overseas entities)?
Why we ask: Protects scope.
Good answer looks like: An explicit exclusion list.

Question: Are any systems changing in the next 12 months (e.g. ERP upgrade, new expense tool)?
Why we ask: A pending change can make a design obsolete.
Follow-up probes:
Dates?
Selected vendor?
Good answer looks like: Planned changes with dates, or none.
Red flags: A replacement under evaluation but not mentioned.

Question: Would you rather get more out of the tools you already have, or are you open to adding a new tool if it removes the work?
Why we ask: Sets the configure-first starting point.
Follow-up probes: Spend range?
Good answer looks like: A clear preference.

Question: Are there limits on budget, IT time, or busy periods we must avoid?
Why we ask: Shapes phasing and session dates.
Follow-up probes: Year end, audit, other projects?
Good answer looks like: Specific limits with dates.

Question: Who would own an automation after go-live?
Why we ask: Every use case needs a run-state owner.
Follow-up probes: Do they have time?
Good answer looks like: A role with capacity.
Red flags: No one.

Question: Who owns each process day to day, and who owns the ERP and IT?
Why we ask: These are the attendees for each session.
Follow-up probes:
Names and roles
who decides?
Good answer looks like: A named owner per process, plus ERP and IT contacts.

Question: Can attendees share their screens and log in to live systems during the sessions?
Why we ask: The live walkthrough needs real screens.
Follow-up probes: Any systems they can't show?
Good answer looks like: Yes for each process owner.
Red flags: Walkthroughs only from slides.

Question: Who can grant us read access or a sandbox, if needed later?
Why we ask: Access lead time often sets a build's start date.
Follow-up probes: In-house or partner?
Good answer looks like: A named role per system.

Question: Are you comfortable with us recording the sessions in Teams and using the transcript (parsed with Copilot or Claude) to prepare notes?
Why we ask: Required under D3 before any recording.
Follow-up probes: Any sessions to exclude?
Good answer looks like: Yes, or the sessions excluded.

Question: Does any of the material we will ask for contain personal information, and are there rules on where it may be stored?
Why we ask: Drives data handling under D3 and the security readiness rating.
Follow-up probes: Employee data in expense exports?
Good answer looks like: Known personal data and any storage rules.

Question: When can we hold the sessions, and how long can each attendee give?
Why we ask: Sets the workshop plan (about half a day per process).
Good answer looks like: Dates for each session.

Question: What are the legal entities in scope, and which country and currency is each in?
Why we ask: Entity count drives configuration effort and intercompany complexity.
Follow-up probes:
Any entities planned or being wound up?
Shared services across entities?
Good answer looks like: A list of entities with country and functional currency.
Red flags: Unclear which entities are in scope.

Question: How is the finance team structured? List roles and how many people are in each.
Why we ask: Tells us who does the work, who reviews it and who will own a solution.
Follow-up probes:
Any vacancies or contractors?
Who covers leave?
Good answer looks like: Roles with headcount, e.g. FC 1, accountants 2, AP 1.
Red flags: One person does everything with no backup.

Question: What do you most want AI and automation to achieve for finance in the next 12 months?
Why we ask: Anchors the recommendation in the client's own words.
Follow-up probes:
Why now?
What has been tried before?
Good answer looks like: Two or three concrete outcomes, e.g. close in 5 days, no manual expense coding.
Red flags: Only 'use AI' with no business outcome.

Question: How will you judge whether this work has been worth it?
Why we ask: Gives us baselines and targets for section 9 success measures.
Follow-up probes:
Hours, errors, days to close, cost?
Who needs convincing?
Good answer looks like: Measurable targets with a baseline.
Red flags: No measure, or a measure no one tracks today.

Question: Are there constraints we must design within, such as budget, IT capacity, timing or change fatigue?
Why we ask: Shapes the delivery tier and phasing.
Follow-up probes:
Any freeze periods (year end, audit)?
Other projects competing for the same people?
Good answer looks like: Specific limits with dates or amounts.
Red flags: Hidden constraints that surface after design sign-off.

Question: List every system finance uses, including spreadsheets that act as systems.
Why we ask: Builds the systems inventory in section 3.
Follow-up probes:
Who owns each?
Which spreadsheets would hurt most if they broke?
Good answer looks like: A complete list including bank portals, expense tools, BI and key workbooks.
Red flags: Key spreadsheets left off the list.

Question: For your ERP and other finance systems, what edition or plan do you have, and which add-on modules?
Why we ask: What is already licensed decides whether we can configure rather than build.
Follow-up probes:
Any modules bought but not used?
When do licences renew?
Good answer looks like: Edition and module list, ideally a screenshot of the licence or billing page.
Red flags: Nobody knows the edition or what is included.

Question: Who administers each system: your own team, an implementation partner or the vendor?
Why we ask: Determines who can make configuration changes and how fast.
Follow-up probes:
How long does a typical change take?
What does a change cost?
Good answer looks like: Named admin per system with turnaround time.
Red flags: Every change goes through a partner with a long queue.

Question: Does your ERP have API or integration access enabled, and is there a sandbox environment?
Why we ask: API access and a sandbox are prerequisites for most automation builds.
Follow-up probes:
Integration records or roles already set up?
Who can grant access?
Good answer looks like: API enabled, sandbox available, an integration role exists.
Red flags: No sandbox; production-only testing.

Question: Which Microsoft 365 licences do you hold, and do you have Copilot, Copilot Studio or Power Automate?
Why we ask: These are often the cheapest route for low-code AI in the client's own environment.
Follow-up probes:
Who manages the M365 tenant?
Are Teams and SharePoint used by finance?
Good answer looks like: Licence types and whether Copilot or Power Platform is available to finance.

Question: Are any AI tools already approved or in use (e.g. Copilot, Claude, ChatGPT), and under what licence?
Why we ask: Reusing an approved tool avoids a new procurement and security review.
Follow-up probes:
Enterprise or personal licences?
Any pilots under way?
Good answer looks like: Approved tools with licence type.
Red flags: Staff using personal AI accounts on company data.

Question: Do you have an AI or acceptable-use policy, and what does it say about financial and employee data?
Why we ask: Feeds the security and privacy readiness rating.
Follow-up probes:
Data residency requirements?
Who approves new tools?
Good answer looks like: A written policy we can read.
Red flags: No policy, or one that bans AI on any company data.

Question: Where must your data be stored or processed, and are there customer or contractual restrictions?
Why we ask: Some contracts restrict where data can go, which limits tool choice.
Follow-up probes: Any government or regulated customers?
Good answer looks like: Clear residency rules, or none.
Red flags: Unknown restrictions discovered after build.

Question: Who in IT would review and approve a new integration or AI tool, and how long does that take?
Why we ask: Approval lead time often sets the start date of a build.
Follow-up probes:
Is there a security questionnaire?
Change advisory board?
Good answer looks like: A named approver and a typical lead time.
Red flags: No one owns the decision.

Question: Would you rather configure the tools you already have, or are you open to adding a new tool if it removes the work?
Why we ask: The configure-first principle depends on the client's answer here.
Follow-up probes:
What monthly cost would be acceptable?
Who signs off new subscriptions?
Good answer looks like: A clear preference with a spend range.
Red flags: Expects automation with no change to tools or process.

Question: After go-live, who in your team would own and maintain an automation?
Why we ask: Every use case needs a named run-state owner before build.
Follow-up probes:
Do they have time?
Any finance systems role?
Good answer looks like: A role with capacity, e.g. systems accountant.
Red flags: No one; the expectation is Deloitte maintains it forever.

Question: What are the biggest pain points you already know about in the processes in scope?
Why we ask: Starts the pain point register before the workshop.
Follow-up probes:
Which one would you fix first?
What has it cost you?
Good answer looks like: Specific pain points with rough impact.

Question: Which features of the tools you already pay for have you not switched on for this process, and why?
Why we ask: The quickest wins are often settings, not AI.
Follow-up probes:
Ever asked the vendor or partner?
Tried and abandoned?
Good answer looks like: Specific features, e.g. auto-categorisation, bank rules.

Question: Who changes the configuration for this process today, and how long does a change take?
Why we ask: Sets realistic effort and ownership for tier 1 changes.
Follow-up probes: Is there a test step before changes go live?
Good answer looks like: A named role and a turnaround time.
Red flags: Changes made directly in production without testing.

Question: If an automation removed most of this work, would you accept a new subscription? Up to what monthly cost?
Why we ask: Tells us whether tier 1, 2 or 3 is acceptable for this process.
Follow-up probes:
Who signs off?
Budget cycle?
Good answer looks like: A yes or no and a spend range.

Question: If this automation stopped working on a Monday morning, who would notice, and who would fix it?
Why we ask: Tests monitoring and run-state ownership before we design.
Follow-up probes:
How would they know?
What would they do in the meantime?
Good answer looks like: A named role and a fallback manual process.
Red flags: No one would notice until month end.

Question: Which steps must a person always review or approve, whatever the technology?
Why we ask: Defines the human-in-the-loop and control points.
Follow-up probes:
Auditor expectations?
Delegated authority limits?
Good answer looks like: Specific review points with thresholds.
Red flags: Wants zero review on postings to the ledger.

Question: Can we get test access to the systems and a set of real sample transactions to build and test against?
Why we ask: No access or data means no build; we need to know now.
Follow-up probes:
Sandbox or production read-only?
Who approves access?
Good answer looks like: Access route agreed with an owner and a date.
Red flags: Access requires a long security process not yet started.

Question: How many expense claims and card transactions do you process each month?
Why we ask: Volume drives the value calculation.
Follow-up probes:
Split claims vs card?
Busiest month?
Good answer looks like: Monthly counts for claims and card lines.

Question: How many employees submit expenses or hold company cards, and does volume peak at any time of year?
Why we ask: Number of submitters drives training and change effort; peaks drive capacity.
Follow-up probes:
Travel-heavy teams?
Year-end spikes?
Good answer looks like: Counts of submitters and cardholders, with peak months.

Question: Which expense tool do you use, and which plan or tier?
Why we ask: Plan tier decides which automation features (card feeds, rules, approvals) are already available.
Follow-up probes:
Any add-ons?
Contract renewal date?
Good answer looks like: Tool and plan name, e.g. Expensify Control.
Red flags: Unknown plan.

Question: Which card provider issues your company cards, and how do card transactions reach the expense tool?
Why we ask: Card feed reliability is a common root cause of capture problems.
Follow-up probes:
Direct bank feed, commercial feed or file upload?
How often do feeds break?
Good answer looks like: Card issuer and feed type with known failure frequency.
Red flags: Feeds break regularly and are fixed by hand.

Question: How do approved expenses get into the ERP: a native connector, a file export, or re-keying?
Why we ask: Defines the integration point and whether coding is lost on the way.
Follow-up probes:
What is created in the ERP: journal, bill, expense report?
Who runs the export?
Good answer looks like: The integration method and the ERP record type created.
Red flags: Manual re-keying of approved claims.

Question: What does your expense policy say about limits, receipts and non-allowable spend, and how is it enforced?
Why we ask: Policy rules become automation rules and exception thresholds.
Follow-up probes:
Policy document available?
Enforced in the tool or by reviewers?
Good answer looks like: A current written policy with limits by category.
Red flags: Policy exists only in people's heads.

Question: Who approves expenses, at what limits, and what happens when an approver is away?
Why we ask: Approval chains are a key control and a frequent bottleneck.
Follow-up probes:
Approver delegation?
Self-approval prevented?
Good answer looks like: An approval matrix with limits and delegates.
Red flags: Approvers approve without looking; no delegation.

Question: How are expenses coded: which dimensions (account, department, class, location, project or job, tax code), and who chooses them?
Why we ask: Coding is usually where effort and errors sit, and where AI suggestion helps most.
Follow-up probes:
Do employees or finance pick the code?
How often is coding corrected?
Good answer looks like: Dimension list with who codes and the correction rate.
Red flags: Most lines recoded by finance at month end.

Question: Is there a mapping from expense categories to GL accounts and tax codes, and can you share it?
Why we ask: We need the mapping to configure or train any auto-coding.
Follow-up probes:
Where is it maintained?
How often does it change?
Good answer looks like: A current mapping table.
Red flags: Mapping held only in the tool with no export.

Question: What share of transactions arrive without a receipt or with an unreadable one, and how do you chase them?
Why we ask: Missing receipts drive chasing effort and tax risk.
Follow-up probes:
How long does chasing take each month?
Any write-offs?
Good answer looks like: An estimate of missing receipts and the chasing effort in hours.
Red flags: Large unreceipted balances at month end.

Question: Walk us through one card transaction from purchase to being posted in the ERP, on screen.
Why we ask: The live walkthrough is the basis of the process card and step map.
Follow-up probes:
Who touches it at each step?
What do you check?
Good answer looks like: Each step with the person, system and time taken.
Red flags: Steps described in theory, not shown.

Question: How many hours a month does each role spend on expenses: submitting, approving, coding, chasing and reconciling?
Why we ask: Gives the effort baseline for value calculations.
Follow-up probes:
Include employee time?
Month-end peak?
Good answer looks like: Hours per role per month.

Question: How do you reconcile the card statement to what was posted, and how often do they not match?
Why we ask: Card reconciliation is a common hidden effort and control gap.
Follow-up probes:
Who signs it off?
Typical differences?
Good answer looks like: A monthly reconciliation with a sign-off and a typical number of differences.
Red flags: No card reconciliation.

Question: How and when are out-of-pocket claims reimbursed, and what is the month-end cut-off?
Why we ask: Cut-off rules affect accruals and posting timing in the design.
Follow-up probes:
Paid via payroll or AP?
Accrual for unsubmitted claims?
Good answer looks like: A reimbursement route and cut-off date.

Question: What goes wrong most often: duplicates, personal spend on company cards, wrong coding, late submission?
Why we ask: Exceptions define where automation needs a human step.
Follow-up probes:
How do you find them?
How long does each take to fix?
Good answer looks like: A ranked list of exceptions with frequency.

Question: Can you export one month of expense reports and card transactions, including the coding applied?
Why we ask: Sample data lets us test feasibility and later the build.
Follow-up probes: Include rejected and corrected lines?
Good answer looks like: An export file with coding and approval status.
Red flags: Export not possible from the current plan.

Question: How many bank accounts do you have, with which banks and currencies, and how many transactions per month on each?
Why we ask: Account count and volume drive matching effort and value.
Follow-up probes:
Any dormant accounts?
Payment gateway or clearing accounts?
Good answer looks like: An account list with bank, currency and monthly lines.

Question: How do bank statements get into the ERP today: direct feed, file download and upload, or manual entry?
Why we ask: The import method is the first thing an automation changes.
Follow-up probes:
Who does it and how often?
How long does it take?
Good answer looks like: The method per account with frequency and time taken.
Red flags: Statements keyed by hand.

Question: Does your bank or ERP offer a direct bank feed, and have you looked at enabling it?
Why we ask: A feed is often a tier 1 configuration win.
Follow-up probes:
Any cost from the bank?
Tried before, and what happened?
Good answer looks like: Feed availability per bank with any cost.

Question: In what file formats can you download statements (CSV, OFX, QIF, CAMT.053, MT940), and do the formats differ by bank?
Why we ask: Format determines how statements are parsed and imported.
Follow-up probes:
Can you share a sample of each?
Any changes planned by the bank?
Good answer looks like: A format per bank, with samples.
Red flags: Only PDF statements available.

Question: Walk us through importing a statement and reconciling it, on screen.
Why we ask: The live walkthrough is the basis of the process card.
Follow-up probes:
Where do you look things up?
What do you write down?
Good answer looks like: Each step with the person, system and time taken.

Question: How are bank lines matched to ERP transactions today, and which matching rules are set up?
Why we ask: Existing rules show what can be configured versus what needs AI suggestion.
Follow-up probes:
Match on amount, reference, date window?
Who maintains rules?
Good answer looks like: A list of current rules and the auto-match rate.
Red flags: Every line matched by hand.

Question: Which items are hardest to match (e.g. batched receipts, card settlements, fees, foreign exchange), and how do you resolve them?
Why we ask: Hard items set the realistic automation share.
Follow-up probes:
How many each month?
How long does each take?
Good answer looks like: Item types with monthly counts and effort.

Question: How do customer receipts get applied to invoices: by bank reference, remittance email or manual lookup?
Why we ask: Cash application often depends on bank data and is a strong AI use case.
Follow-up probes:
Remittance advices emailed?
Share of receipts with no reference?
Good answer looks like: The method with the share of receipts needing manual lookup.

Question: Who prepares and who reviews bank reconciliations, how often, and how is sign-off evidenced?
Why we ask: Defines controls the automation must keep.
Follow-up probes:
Audit findings in the last year?
Unreconciled items older than 30 days?
Good answer looks like: Preparer, reviewer, frequency and evidence of sign-off.
Red flags: Same person prepares and reviews.

Question: How quickly after the bank date are transactions imported and reconciled, daily and at month end?
Why we ask: Timeliness is a common pain point and success measure.
Follow-up probes:
Backlog today?
Target?
Good answer looks like: Days behind, daily and at month end.
Red flags: Reconciliation only done at month end.

Question: Can you share three months of statements in their native format, plus the matching ERP report for the same period?
Why we ask: Lets us measure the achievable auto-match rate before design.
Follow-up probes: Include all accounts?
Good answer looks like: Native statement files and an ERP export for the same months.
Red flags: Only PDF or screenshots.

Question: Who can grant access to the bank portal and the ERP bank import features, and is two-factor authentication tied to a person?
Why we ask: Personal two-factor often blocks automated downloads.
Follow-up probes: Is there a service account option?
Good answer looks like: An access route that does not depend on one person's phone.
Red flags: Downloads depend on one person's two-factor device.

Question: Who uses the cash flow forecast, for what decisions, and how often?
Why we ask: Purpose decides horizon, granularity and accuracy needed.
Follow-up probes:
Bank covenant reporting?
Board?
Good answer looks like: Named consumers and decisions, e.g. weekly treasury call.
Red flags: Forecast prepared but rarely used.

Question: What horizon and granularity does the forecast cover (e.g. 13 weeks weekly, 12 months monthly), and how often is it refreshed?
Why we ask: Defines the model structure and refresh cadence.
Follow-up probes: Different views for different audiences?
Good answer looks like: Horizon, buckets and refresh frequency.

Question: Where is the forecast built today, and who owns the model?
Why we ask: Spreadsheet models are a key-person risk and a common starting point.
Follow-up probes:
How many tabs and links?
Version control?
Good answer looks like: Tool and owner, with the model file.
Red flags: One person built it and no one else understands it.

Question: Which inputs feed the forecast: AR ageing, AP ageing, payroll, tax, capex, debt, sales orders, pipeline?
Why we ask: Each input is a data source the automation must read.
Follow-up probes:
Which are automated today?
Which are estimates?
Good answer looks like: Each input with its source system and how it is pulled.

Question: For each input, how is the data pulled into the model: report export, copy-paste or typed?
Why we ask: Data movement is usually most of the refresh effort.
Follow-up probes: How long does each take?
Good answer looks like: A method and time per input.

Question: Which assumptions drive the forecast (e.g. debtor days, payment runs, seasonality), and how are they set and reviewed?
Why we ask: Assumptions become drivers in a driver-based forecast.
Follow-up probes:
Who approves them?
When were they last updated?
Good answer looks like: Documented drivers with an owner.
Red flags: Assumptions hard-coded and undocumented.

Question: Walk us through one forecast refresh from start to finished output, on screen.
Why we ask: The live walkthrough is the basis of the process card.
Follow-up probes: What do you check before sending?
Good answer looks like: Each step with the person, system and time taken.

Question: How many hours does each refresh take, and who does it?
Why we ask: Gives the effort baseline.
Follow-up probes: Month-end refresh longer?
Good answer looks like: Hours per refresh per role.

Question: Do you compare forecast to actual, and how accurate has the forecast been?
Why we ask: Accuracy tracking is a value driver and success measure.
Follow-up probes: Main reasons for variance?
Good answer looks like: A variance history with reasons.
Red flags: No actual-versus-forecast comparison.

Question: Do you need scenarios or sensitivities (e.g. a large customer pays late), and how are they produced today?
Why we ask: Scenario needs change the design and tool choice.
Follow-up probes:
Who asks for them?
How often?
Good answer looks like: Scenario types and frequency.

Question: Who writes commentary on the forecast and on variances, and how long does it take?
Why we ask: Commentary generation is a common AI use case.
Follow-up probes: Audience for commentary?
Good answer looks like: Author, audience and time taken.

Question: Can you share the current forecast model and the last three months of forecast versus actual?
Why we ask: Lets us assess model structure and accuracy before design.
Follow-up probes: Include assumptions tab?
Good answer looks like: The model file and variance history.

Question: How many items does this process handle each month, and what counts as one item (e.g. an invoice, a journal, a reconciliation)?
Why we ask: Volume drives the value calculation; the unit must be explicit.
Follow-up probes:
Busiest month?
Split by type?
Good answer looks like: A monthly count with its unit.

Question: Does volume peak at certain times (month end, year end, season)?
Why we ask: Peaks drive capacity and the design's tolerance for delay.
Good answer looks like: Peak months with rough volumes.

Question: How often does the process run, and what are its deadlines?
Why we ask: Frequency and deadlines define the cycle and the timing the solution must meet.
Follow-up probes: Working-day targets at month end?
Good answer looks like: Frequency with deadlines, e.g. daily, done by WD+3.

Question: Which systems, spreadsheets and mailboxes does this process use?
Why we ask: Builds the system list for this process.
Follow-up probes: Any spreadsheet only one person understands?
Good answer looks like: Every system and file touched.

Question: How does data move between those systems: integration, file upload, re-keying or email?
Why we ask: Manual data movement is where most use cases come from.
Follow-up probes: Who does it, how often, how long?
Good answer looks like: A method per hand-off.
Red flags: Re-keying between systems.

Question: What starts the process, and what marks it as finished?
Why we ask: Defines the boundaries of the process card.
Good answer looks like: A clear start trigger and end point.

Question: Walk us through one real, recent item from start to finish, on screen.
Why we ask: The live walkthrough is the basis of the process card.
Follow-up probes:
Who touches it at each step?
What do you check?
Good answer looks like: Each step with the person, system and time taken.
Red flags: Steps described in theory, not shown.

Question: Which rules decide how items are coded, matched, approved or routed?
Why we ask: Rules become configuration or automation logic.
Follow-up probes:
Written down anywhere?
Who maintains them?
Good answer looks like: Documented rules with an owner.
Red flags: Rules only in one person's head.

Question: Who reviews and approves the work, at what limits, and how is sign-off evidenced?
Why we ask: Controls the automation must keep.
Follow-up probes: Same person prepares and reviews?
Good answer looks like: Reviewer, limits and evidence of sign-off.
Red flags: No review or no evidence.

Question: What goes wrong most often, how is it found, and how long does it take to fix?
Why we ask: Exceptions define where a person stays in the loop.
Follow-up probes: What went wrong last month?
Good answer looks like: A ranked list of exceptions with frequency and effort.

Question: How many hours per cycle does each role spend on this process?
Why we ask: Gives the effort baseline for value calculations.
Follow-up probes: Including chasing and rework?
Good answer looks like: Hours per role per cycle.

Question: Which parts involve copying, re-keying, looking things up or chasing people?
Why we ask: Manual touchpoints are the candidates for automation.
Good answer looks like: Each touchpoint with time taken.

Question: Can you export one month of the items this process handles, with the outcome of each (coded, matched, approved)?
Why we ask: Sample data lets us test feasibility and later the build.
Follow-up probes: Include exceptions and corrections?
Good answer looks like: An export with outcomes.
Red flags: No export possible.

Question: Are there procedures, checklists or policies for this process you can share?
Why we ask: Speeds up the draft process card and the rules.
Good answer looks like: Current written procedures.
